sentences.text: The name Pliosaurus means "more lizard" because the animal's appearance was considered more reminiscent of crocodilians than of Plesiosaurus.
A main diagnostic trait of the genus is that its teeth are robust and have a trihedral cross-section.
The largest species, P. funkei and P. kevani, are estimated to reach around 10 meters in length and weigh nearly 11 tonnes, with skulls exceeding 2 meters in length.
Based on morphological and histological characteristics like increased bone density, the two specimens of P. funkei appear to have been adults.
Re-examination of the Svalbard specimen fossils revised the estimated total length to a range of 10.0 to 12.8 meters.
Although mentioned in 1824, Pliosaurus was not formally described until 1841 by Richard Owen, who first placed it in Plesiosaurus and later established it as its own genus.

In 1841, Richard Owen described the Market Rasen specimen as the holotype of a new species, Plesiosaurus (Pleiosaurus) brachydeirus, where the specific name refers to the short cervical vertebrae of the specimen.
In 1871, John Phillips recognized P. brachydeirus as the type species and used the original spelling Pleiosaurus.
Pliosaurus used its long, robust snouts to capture large prey by piercing them with numerous trihedral teeth located at the back of the jaws.
Analysis of the four flipper bones suggests the animal swam using only its two front flippers, using the rear pair only for extra thrust when chasing and capturing prey.
Harry Govier Seeley named the family Pliosauridae in 1874 to include forms similar to Pliosaurus.
Phylogenetic classifications place Pliosaurus in a derived position within the Thalassophonea, often related to Gallardosaurus.
Since a 2013 paper, only six species have been firmly recognized as valid within the genus Pliosaurus.
Two additional species from Argentina named in 2014 and 2018 have not been fully confirmed as belonging to the genus in subsequent classifications.
Pliosaurus fossils range from the Late Jurassic to the Lower Cretaceous, specifically from the Kimmeridgian to the Valanginian stages, with a possible record from the Oxfordian.
Pliosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic in what is now Europe and South America.
Pliosaurus portentificus originates from the late Kimmeridgian of England.
Knutsen and colleagues suggest that P. funkei and P. rossicus might represent different growth stages of the same species, though they maintain them as distinct taxa.
Benson and colleagues argue that morphological differences between two Westbury specimens justify classifying them as separate species rather than intraspecific variation.
Knutsen maintains the validity of P. brachyspondylus and P. macromerus based on proposed neotypes, though their original types are non-diagnostic.
P. andrewsi is no longer considered a valid species of Pliosaurus due to having too many morphological differences.
